extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, critics, and writers studying humor and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze criteria that make language and character comic: mechanisms (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition), stylistic keys (solemn/familiar, jargon, parody, exaggeration), and character conditions (unsociability, automatism, gesture vs action, emotional insulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms that make series of words comic
rubrics_metrics.description: "Series of events" may become comic either by repetition, by inversion, or by reciprocal interference; the same three general propositions apply to series of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat verbal sequences like comic situations: repeat phrases in another key/environment; invert elements while preserving some sense; mix meanings so they jostle. These are general, reusable devices across styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (verbal repetition as comic device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition consists in arranging speech so a phrase or scene is reproduced under fresh circumstances (e.g., a lackey repeating a master's scene in less dignified language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition to create mismatch between form and context; reproduce an expression or situation in a different register or with different participants to reveal comic incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (reversing sentence roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inversion: experiment by reversing a sentence (putting subject in place of object and vice versa) to obtain a new meaning; commonly used by wits to refute or lampoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple to apply; can produce quick witty retorts (example: 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' — 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference / play upon words
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal interference: bracketing two independent meanings in the same expression; ranges from puns (different words, same sound) to true play upon words (one sentence expressing two idea-sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pun is 'least reputable' (phonetic equivocation). True word-play exploits multiple senses of a single sentence/word (figurative vs literal). It often signals a momentary lapse or negligence in language, which produces amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (comic transformation of sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: 'A comic effect is always obtainable by transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key.' Transposition moves an idea into an inappropriate stylistic key or environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many means and stages exist (from buffoonery to refined irony). It's sufficient to present only the transposed expression, since audiences supply the natural expression by familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposing the solemn into the familiar → Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Transpose the solemn into the familiar and you obtain parody; expressing dignified or classical matter in familiar or modern terms produces comic effect (example: 'The sky ... like a lobster being boiled').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody often reads as degradation of the dignified, but is better understood as a form of transposition; use incongruous register shift from high to low for parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposing the familiar into the solemn / Exaggeration / Mock-heroic
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of small things as though they were large is exaggeration; prolonged/systematic exaggeration yields comic effect and gives rise to mock-heroic tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration should be sustained or systematic to be comic; methodical bragging or inflated diction applied to trivial subjects produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition upwards in moral value (respectable diction for disreputable matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing scandalous, low-class, or disgraceful situations in terms of utmost respectability (transposing moral value upwards) is generally comic (common in English literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single respectable word can evoke an entire transposition system within social circles (example: 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank'). Use polite/formal diction to describe base behavior to reveal absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between real and ideal: Irony vs Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: When transposition deals with the real vs the ideal: stating what ought to be and feigning belief it's what is (irony), versus describing what is and pretending it's what ought to be (humour). Irony is oratorical; humour is scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use irony to elevate the moral ideal and show its absence; use humour to catalogue or dissect the real in concrete, technical detail, producing detachment rather than moral uplift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition into professional/technical jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into a profession's technical vocabulary or business phraseology (e.g., applying commercial formulas to social relations) produces comic effects and can reveal character faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ specialized jargon in inappropriate social contexts to highlight mechanisation of feeling (example: 'Your kindness of the third ult.'), and use it to satirize a character's outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic depends on preventing audience emotion (appeals to intelligence, not feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter 'appeals to the intelligence' and is incompatible with emotion; to make a fault or vice comic the poet must prevent sympathy, pity, or fear from arising in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques to blunt sympathy include isolating the feeling, focusing on mechanical gestures, or otherwise making the feeling unparasitic so it doesn't contagiously move spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate feeling within character (parasitic emotion) to avoid sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: First method for neutralizing sympathy: make the feeling within the character parasitic and isolated, so it neither impregnates other mental states nor becomes contagious; the emotion remains a stranger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict feelings as rigid fragments that do not color the whole personality (example: Harpagon's greed passes by without touching other feelings), which makes them comic rather than tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gestures rather than actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy directs attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, language expressing without conscious aim) rather than actions (intentional, conscious deeds); gestures are automatic and explosive, preventing serious engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters' outer signs (automatized attitudes, set phrases, habitual movements) salient. Gestural emphasis turns potentially serious motives into comic spectacle (example: Tartuffe's mechanical pious phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsociability as essential condition of comic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual who automatically goes his own way without adapting to social surroundings (unsociability) is liable to be comic; comedy reproves absentmindedness and rigidity by social snubbing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters whose habits, rigidities, or withdrawal from social norms mark them as unable to fit in; their lack of adaptability is the source of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / absentmindedness as the core of the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically: involuntary gestures, unconscious remarks, systematic absentmindedness (e.g., Don Quixote) betray the person and are the deepest source of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize unconscious, mechanical behavior and habitual rigidity. The more automatic and pervasive the absentmindedness, the stronger the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity vs flexibility: comic arises from rigidity relative to social ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigidity (in vice or virtue) rather than the moral quality itself provokes laughter; a rigid virtue may be ludicrous because it marks unsociability, whereas flexibility avoids ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight one-sidedness or inflexibility in a character's traits (even honestly moral traits) to render them comic; show how social maladjustment, not moral failing per se, invites laughter.
